title: What you pay: premium
teaches: The premium is the option's price, quoted per share and paid per contract (usually 100 shares); buying opens a debit and caps your loss at the premium, selling opens a credit that caps your gain, not your loss.

facts.quote: When you buy an option, the purchase price is called the premium. If you sell, the premium is the amount you receive.
facts.claim: The premium is the option's price: the buyer pays it and the seller receives it.

facts.quote: The premium isn't fixed and changes constantly.
facts.claim: An option's premium is not fixed; it changes all the time.

facts.quote: Changing prices reflect the give and take between what buyers are willing to pay and what sellers are willing to accept for the option.
facts.claim: The premium moves with what buyers will pay and what sellers will accept.

facts.quote: If you buy options, you begin with a net debit. That means you've spent money you might never recover if you don't sell your option at a profit or exercise it.
facts.claim: Buying an option opens with a net debit: money spent that you may never get back.

facts.quote: If you do make money on a transaction, you must subtract the cost of the premium from any income to find net profit.
facts.claim: Your profit is what you take in minus the premium you paid.

facts.quote: As a seller, you begin with a net credit because you collect the premium. If the option is never exercised, you keep the money.
facts.claim: Selling an option opens with a net credit: you collect the premium and keep it if the option is never exercised.

facts.quote: All market participants affect the price of an options through the process of supply and demand where buyers and sellers come together creating best bid/ask of all bids and offers.
facts.claim: Option prices come from supply and demand, shown as the best bid and ask.

facts.quote: Equity option contracts usually represent 100 shares of the underlying stock.
facts.claim: A stock option contract usually covers 100 shares.

facts.quote: Buyers and sellers set option prices in the exchange markets.
facts.claim: Buyers and sellers on the exchanges set option prices.

facts.quote: An option's price is called the premium and is priced at a per share basis. The option holder’s potential loss is limited to the initial premium paid for the contract.
facts.claim: The premium is quoted per share, and a buyer's loss is limited to the premium paid.

facts.quote: the writer collects the premium and has theoretically unlimited loss potential for a call option and substantial loss potential for a put option.
facts.claim: A seller collects the premium but can lose without limit on a call and a lot on a put.

facts.quote: Factors having a significant effect on options premium include: Underlying price Strike Time until expiration Implied volatility Dividends Interest rate
facts.claim: The premium is driven by the stock price, the strike, time to expiry, implied volatility, dividends and interest rates.

facts.quote: Dividends and risk-free interest rate have a lesser effect.
facts.claim: Dividends and interest rates move the premium less than the other factors.

facts.quote: These price changes have opposite effects on calls and puts. For instance, as the value of the underlying security rises, a call will generally increase. However, the value of a put will generally decrease in price.
facts.claim: A rising stock generally lifts calls and lowers puts.

facts.quote: Higher volatility estimates indicate greater expected fluctuations (in either direction) in underlying price levels. This expectation generally results in higher option premiums for puts and calls alike.
facts.claim: Higher expected movement generally means higher premiums for calls and puts.

facts.quote: Generally, as expiration approaches, the levels of an option's time value decrease or erode for both puts and calls.
facts.claim: Time value generally erodes as expiry approaches, for calls and puts.

facts.quote: if the owner's options expire with no value, this loss can be the entire amount of the premium paid for the option. An uncovered option writer may face unlimited risk.
facts.claim: A buyer whose options expire worthless loses the whole premium; an uncovered writer can face unlimited risk.

facts.quote: For a put, the fact that the stock cannot fall below $0 in price limits the risk of loss. This potential loss could still be quite large if the underlying stock declines significantly in price.
facts.claim: A put seller's loss stops at a stock price of zero, but it can still be very large.

facts.quote: As an options holder, you risk the entire amount of the premium you pay.
facts.claim: An option buyer risks the whole premium paid.

facts.quote: if you write an uncovered call, you face unlimited potential loss, since there is no cap on how high a stock price can rise.
facts.claim: Writing an uncovered call carries unlimited risk because a stock has no price ceiling.

facts.quote: An option holder cannot lose more than the initial price paid for the option.
facts.claim: An option buyer cannot lose more than the price paid.

facts.quote: it might make sense to sell the call while it still has some time value. A timely decision might allow the investor to recoup some or even all of the investment.
facts.claim: Selling a losing call while it still has value can recover part of what you paid.

facts.quote: Since this investor did not originally set aside the cash to buy the stock, an unexpected exercise could be a major inconvenience and require urgent measures to come up with the cash for settlement.
facts.claim: If a call is exercised and you haven't set aside cash for the shares, you have to find it fast.

facts.quote: The strike price of the short call is higher than the strike of the long call, which means this strategy will always require an initial outlay (debit).
facts.claim: A bull call spread always opens as a debit.

facts.quote: The short call's main purpose is to help pay for the long call's upfront cost.
facts.claim: The call you sell in a bull call spread helps pay for the call you buy.

facts.quote: Because of the relationship between the two strike prices, the investor will always receive a premium (credit) when initiating this position.
facts.claim: A bull put spread always opens as a credit.

facts.quote: The most this spread can earn is the net premium received at the outset
facts.claim: The most a bull put spread can make is the credit received.

facts.quote: The maximum loss is the difference between the strikes, less the credit received when putting on the position.
facts.claim: A bull put spread's maximum loss is the strike width minus the credit.

facts.quote: The bull call spread requires a known initial outlay for an unknown eventual return; the bull put spread produces a known initial cash inflow in exchange for a possible outlay later on.
facts.claim: A debit spread pays out cash now; a credit spread takes cash in now but may cost money later.

facts.quote: The premium is the price that the holder of an option pays and the writer of an option receives for the rights conveyed by the option.
facts.claim: The premium is what the buyer pays and the seller receives for the option's rights.

facts.quote: The premium does not constitute a “down-payment.”
facts.claim: The premium is not a down payment on the shares.

facts.quote: The premium is not fixed by the options markets or by OCC.
facts.claim: Neither the exchanges nor the OCC fix the premium.

facts.quote: the unit of trading for most options on equity securities is 100 shares.
facts.claim: Most stock options trade in units of 100 shares.

facts.quote: If the option is trading at a premium of, say, $4 per share, then the aggregate premium for a single option contract would be $400.
facts.claim: A premium of 4 dollars a share means 400 dollars for one contract.

facts.quote: In June an investor buys a December XYZ 50 call at an aggregate premium of $500.
facts.claim: In the example, the investor pays 500 dollars in total for the call.

facts.quote: if by September the market price of the option has decreased to $300, the investor might still decide to sell the option in a closing transaction, thereby limiting his loss to $200.
facts.claim: When the call falls to 300 dollars, selling it to close limits the loss to 200 dollars.

facts.quote: An option holder runs the risk of losing the entire amount paid for the option in a relatively short period of time.
facts.claim: A buyer can lose everything paid for an option, and fast.

facts.quote: An investor receives a premium of $4 a share for writing an uncovered XYZ 50 call option and the stock price jumps to $69 as the option approaches expiration.
facts.claim: In the example, a 4-dollar uncovered call is written and the stock jumps to 69.

facts.quote: If the investor liquidates his option position at, say, $19, in an offsetting closing purchase transaction, he will incur a loss of $1,500 (the $1,900 paid in the offsetting purchase transaction less the $400 option premium
facts.claim: Buying it back at 19 loses 1,500 dollars: 1,900 paid less the 400 collected.

facts.quote: The writer of a put option bears a risk of loss if the value of the underlying interest declines below the exercise price, and such loss could be substantial if the decline is significant
facts.claim: A put seller loses if the stock falls below the strike, and the loss can be large.

facts.quote: A writer of a physical delivery put who is assigned an exercise must purchase the underlying interest at the exercise price
facts.claim: An assigned put seller must buy the shares at the strike.

facts.quote: Investor C invests his entire $5,000 in 10 XYZ 50 calls.
facts.claim: Investor C puts the whole 5,000 dollars into 10 calls.

facts.quote: Investor B invests $500 in the purchase of an XYZ 50 call (covering 100 shares of XYZ at a premium of $5 a share)
facts.claim: Investor B spends 500 dollars on one call at 5 dollars a share.

facts.quote: would lose all of his investment if the price of XYZ stayed at or below 50.
facts.claim: Investor C loses everything if the stock ends at or below 50.

facts.quote: The impact of transaction costs on profitability is often greater for options transactions than for transactions in the underlying interests because these costs are often greater in relation to options premiums
facts.claim: Commissions often weigh more on options than on stock because they are large next to the premium.

facts.quote: The transaction costs of options investing consist primarily of commissions (which are imposed in opening, closing, exercise and assignment transactions)
facts.claim: Options trades cost commissions to open, close, exercise and be assigned.

facts.quote: A standard-size options contract is equal to 100 shares of the underlying security.
facts.claim: A standard options contract equals 100 shares.

facts.quote: For the purchaser of an option, the premium paid is your maximum loss. For the seller of an option, the premium you receive at the time of the sale is your maximum profit.
facts.claim: A buyer's maximum loss is the premium paid; a seller's maximum profit is the premium received.

facts.quote: In the case of an uncovered, or naked, call, where an investor sells a call option without owning the underlying stock, the maximum loss is theoretically unlimited.
facts.claim: Selling a call without owning the stock has a theoretically unlimited maximum loss.

facts.quote: The premium is a nonrefundable payment in full from the purchaser to the seller in exchange for the rights conveyed by the option.
facts.claim: The premium is paid in full and never refunded.

facts.quote: Because one options contract is tied to 100 shares of stock, exercising a call can require substantial funds. For a contract with a strike price of $100, the owner of a call would need $10,000 to exercise.
facts.claim: Exercising one call costs the strike times 100: 10,000 dollars for a 100 strike.

facts.quote: carried "long" in a customer's account that expires in nine months or less, initial margin must be deposited and maintained equal to at least 100 percent of the purchase price of the option
facts.claim: Under FINRA's rule, an option you buy that expires in nine months or less must be paid for in full.

facts.quote: "Long" options must be paid for in full. The proceeds of the "short" options may be applied towards the cost of the "long" options and/or any margin requirement.
facts.claim: In a spread, the options you buy are paid in full, and the premium from the ones you sell can go toward that cost.

facts.quote: an option seller could expect to receive a total premium of $790 ($7.90 premium x 100 shares) and an option buyer could expect to pay a total premium of $800 ($8.00 premium x 100 shares)
facts.claim: With bid 7.90 and ask 8.00, a seller receives 790 dollars and a buyer pays 800 dollars per contract.

facts.quote: An option has a bid of $7.90 and an ask of $8.00.
facts.claim: The example quote is bid 7.90, ask 8.00.

facts.quote: Options buyers focus on the ask price as it represents the cost and risk of purchasing an option. Sellers focus on the bid price, which is the premium received for taking on the contract's risk.
facts.claim: A buyer pays the ask and a seller receives the bid.

facts.quote: Sell the call option and lock in a theoretical profit of $400 ($5 sale − $1 purchase = $4 profit x 100 shares = $400.)
facts.claim: Profit on one contract is sale price minus purchase price, times 100.

facts.quote: Buy 1 JKL 100 call at (3.30) Sell 1 JKL 105 call at 1.50 Net cost = (1.80)
facts.claim: Buying a call at 3.30 and selling a higher-strike call at 1.50 nets a cost of 1.80 a share.

facts.quote: the term “debit” refers to the fact that the strategy is created for a net cost, or net debit.
facts.claim: A debit spread is one that costs you money to open.

facts.quote: Sell 1 JKL 100 put at 3.20 Buy 1 JKL 95 put at (1.30) Net credit = 1.90
facts.claim: Selling a put at 3.20 and buying a lower-strike put at 1.30 nets a credit of 1.90 a share.

facts.quote: The term “credit” refers to the fact that the strategy is created for a net credit, or net amount received.
facts.claim: A credit spread is one that pays you money to open.

facts.quote: The maximum risk is equal to the difference between the strike prices minus the net credit received including commissions.
facts.claim: A bull put spread's maximum risk is the strike width minus the net credit.

facts.quote: When an investor exercises a call option, the net price paid for the underlying stock on a per share basis is the sum of the call's strike price plus the premium paid for the call.
facts.claim: Shares bought by exercising a call really cost the strike plus the premium paid.

facts.quote: Readers should not assume that options premiums will necessarily conform or correlate with any theoretical options pricing formula, chart, last sale, or the prices of the underlying interest, related interests or other options at any particular time.
facts.claim: A premium need not match the last sale, a formula or a chart at any moment.

facts.quote: an investor who has written a call contract is assigned an exercise notice on that call, the net price received on per share basis is the sum of the call's strike price plus the premium received
facts.claim: An assigned call seller receives the strike for the shares, plus the premium collected earlier.

facts.quote: Options occasionally; no further rules. The premium paid is the stop.
facts.claim: Rule B25: we use options occasionally, and on an option we buy the premium paid is the stop.

facts.quote: Trade shares; options are only a defined-risk alternative.
facts.claim: Rule A6: we trade shares, and we use options only as a defined-risk alternative.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62)
facts.claim: Rule A3: on a share trade the stop comes first, by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low.

facts.quote: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy
facts.claim: Rule A13: on a share trade the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

walkthroughs.title: A quote is per share
steps: Pull up an option chain. Every price on it is per share, not per contract.
Most stock option contracts cover 100 shares. So you multiply the quote by 100.
A $4 quote costs you $400 for one contract, plus commissions. Price the contract, never the quote.

walkthroughs.title: Debit or credit
steps: Buying opens with a debit. The premium leaves your account, and you may never get it back.
Sell one to open and it's a credit. The premium comes in. That's the seller's side, not ours.
With two legs, net them. Pay 3.30 for a call, collect 1.50 selling a higher one. You're out 1.80, a debit.
Collect more than you pay and it's a credit. Money comes in the day you open it.

walkthroughs.title: What each side can lose
steps: As a buyer, the most you can lose is what you paid, plus commissions. The premium is your stop.
The seller's best case is keeping the premium they collected. That's as good as it gets for them.
Their worst case is far bigger. Write a call without owning the stock and the loss has no ceiling.

questions.q: You pull up an option chain and every call and put has a premium next to it. What is the premium?
questions.why: It's the option's price. That's all premium means. You buy, you pay it. You sell, you collect it. It moves all day, same as the stock does. It's not the strike. The strike is where the shares change hands if the option gets exercised. And it's not a deposit or a commission. Get this word down, because everything else in options runs on it.
questions.lesson_line: Premium is the price. Buyer pays it, seller keeps it.

wrong.The broker's commission: Commissions are a separate cost. The premium goes from the buyer to the seller.
wrong.The contract's strike price: The strike is the price the shares trade at if the option is exercised. The premium is what the option itself costs.
wrong.A deposit on the shares: It's not a down payment on anything. It buys the right, and that's all it buys.

questions.simple: The premium is just the option's price. The buyer pays it and the seller collects it.

questions.q: You buy a call, the stock goes nowhere, and the call expires. Your broker refunds the premium you paid.
questions.why: False. That money's gone. You pay the premium in full to the seller the day you buy, and it never comes back as a refund. It's what the right cost you, not a deposit. The only ways to get any of it back are selling the option while it still has value, or exercising it. Let it expire worthless and you've lost all of it. So I count the premium as spent the moment the order fills.
questions.lesson_line: Premium spent is spent. Count it as gone the day you buy.
questions.simple: False. The premium is paid in full and never refunded, even when the option expires worthless.

questions.q: Fill in the blank.
questions.sentence: Stock option prices are quoted per ___.
questions.why: Share. An option's price, the premium, is quoted on a per share basis. Equity option contracts usually cover 100 shares, so one contract usually costs 100 times the quote. It is not quoted per contract, per day or per lot.
questions.lesson_line: Read every option quote as per share. The contract is 100 times that.
questions.simple: Stock option prices are quoted per share, and one contract usually covers 100 shares.

questions.q: A call you like is quoted at 1.50 on the chain. You buy one contract. What actually leaves your account, before commissions?
questions.why: $150. Option quotes are per share, and one standard contract covers 100 shares. So 1.50 times 100 is $150 for one contract, with commissions on top. This trips up a lot of new traders. They see 1.50, think it's cheap, and buy ten. That's $1,500 going out, not $15. Price the contract, never the quote.
questions.lesson_line: Price the contract, not the quote. That's what leaves your account.

wrong.$1.50: That's the quote, one share's worth. A contract covers 100 shares.
wrong.$15: That's a tenth of it. A contract covers 100 shares.
wrong.$1,500: That's ten contracts. You bought one.

questions.simple: $150. The 1.50 quote is per share and one contract covers 100 shares.

questions.q: You sell to open one put and the order fills. What happens in your account right then?
questions.why: Cash comes in. You sold, so the buyer pays you the premium the moment it fills. That's a credit. Buying is the reverse, the premium leaves and you start with a debit. The strike only matters if you get assigned. Then, as the put seller, you have to buy the shares at the strike. That's the part that can hurt, and it's why selling is never free money. Selling to open isn't something we do. On the rare option we use, we're the buyer, so we start with the debit.
questions.lesson_line: Sell to open and cash comes in. Buy to open and it goes out.

wrong.Nothing until expiry: You collect the premium when the sale fills, not at expiry.
wrong.Cash goes out, a debit: That's how a buyer starts. You sold, so the premium comes to you.
wrong.You pay the strike: Only if you're assigned. Then you buy the shares at the strike. Not when the sale fills.

questions.simple: Selling to open pays you the premium when it fills, so you start with a credit.

questions.q: You buy one call. However badly it goes, the most you can lose on that call is what you paid, plus commissions.
questions.why: True. As a buyer, your worst case is the premium. The call can go to zero, but not below it, so you can't lose more than you put in. Add the commissions to open and close. One catch. If you exercise, you're buying the shares, and that takes real cash and brings new risk. That's a separate trade. On the call itself, the premium is the most you lose, so I size it like a loss I'll take in full.
questions.lesson_line: Buy an option and the premium is your worst case. Size it like a loss you'll take.
questions.simple: True. A buyer can lose at most the premium paid, with commissions on top.

questions.q: A buddy sells to open one call and collects the premium. Then the stock falls hard. What's the most he can make on that call?
questions.why: The premium he collected. The best thing that can happen to a call seller is the call expiring worthless. He keeps the premium and that's it, however far the stock drops. Now flip it. If the stock rips and he doesn't own the shares, his loss has no ceiling. A small, capped gain against an open-ended loss. We leave that trade to others. When we buy an option, it's the other way around. The premium is the most we can lose.
questions.lesson_line: A call seller's best case is the premium. Without the shares, his worst case has no ceiling.

wrong.Unlimited, if the stock falls: A falling stock just makes the call worthless. He keeps the premium, and that's his ceiling.
wrong.The strike price times 100: That's what he'd be paid for the shares if he's assigned. It's not profit on the option.
wrong.The rise above the strike: A rise above the strike is his loss as the seller, not his gain.

questions.simple: A call seller makes at most the premium collected, however far the stock falls.

questions.q: You're watching a call on the chain and its price jumps from one minute to the next. Who's setting that premium?
choices: The company that issued the stock
questions.why: Buyers and sellers, trading it. The premium is a market price, same as the stock. It moves with what buyers will pay and what sellers will take, all day long. The exchange is just where they meet. It doesn't set the price. Neither does the OCC, the clearing house behind listed options. So when a premium jumps, the market just repriced it. Often the stock moved first. Read it like you'd read the stock's own bid and ask.
questions.lesson_line: Nobody hands you the premium. It's a market price, and it moves.

wrong.The OCC, once a day: The OCC clears the trades. It doesn't fix the price, and the price changes all day.
wrong.The exchange, at listing: The exchange is where buyers and sellers meet. They set the price, not the exchange.
wrong.The company that issued the stock: The company has no say in its option prices. Buyers and sellers set them.

questions.simple: Buyers and sellers set the premium by trading it, so it moves all day like any market price.

questions.q: You're holding a call for a few weeks. Which of these moves its premium the least?
questions.why: The interest rate. Price, time and volatility do the heavy lifting. The stock moving is the big one. Time matters because time value wears away as expiry gets closer. Volatility matters because bigger expected moves cost more. Rates and dividends count too, just a lot less. So when your call moves, look at the stock, the calendar and volatility first.
questions.lesson_line: Price, time and volatility drive the premium. Rates count, just a lot less.

wrong.The stock price: That's the biggest driver of all. Rates matter far less.
wrong.Time to expiry: Time is a big one. Time value wears away as expiry gets closer.
wrong.Volatility: Volatility is a big one. Bigger expected moves mean pricier calls and puts.

questions.simple: The interest rate. Rates and dividends move the premium far less than price, time and volatility.

questions.q: You want 3 calls quoted at 2.40. Before you hit buy, what's the total cost, before commissions?
questions.why: $720. Do it in steps. The 2.40 quote is per share, and one contract is 100 shares. So 2.40 times 100 is $240 a contract. You want 3, and $240 times 3 is $720. Commissions come on top. Run that math before every order. It's the number at risk if the calls expire worthless, so it's what you size off.
questions.lesson_line: Quote, times 100, times contracts. Do it before every order.
questions.simple: $720. The 2.40 quote is per share, each contract is 100 shares, and you're buying 3.

wrong.$7.20: That's the quote times 3. Each contract is 100 shares.
wrong.$7,200: A decimal slipped. 2.40 times 100 times 3 is $720.

questions.q: You own a put. The stock rallies hard and nothing else changes. Your put is now worth less than before.
questions.why: True. A put pays when the stock falls, so a rally works against it. Calls are the mirror image, and the same rally lifts them. That's the answer with everything else held still. In real life volatility moves too, and a jump in volatility lifts calls and puts alike. So a put can hold up better than you'd expect on a rally. But the stock's direction is the first thing you check.
questions.lesson_line: Stock up, calls up, puts down. Then check what volatility did.
questions.simple: True. A rising stock lifts calls and pushes puts down, all else equal.

questions.story: You buy 2 calls at 3.10. In the same order, you sell 2 higher-strike calls at 1.25. Same stock, same expiry.
questions.q: The order fills. Does cash go out or come in, and how much, before commissions?
questions.why: A $370 debit, so cash goes out. Net the legs first. You pay 3.10 and collect 1.25, and 3.10 minus 1.25 is 1.85 a share. Times 100 shares is $185 a spread. You did 2, so $370 leaves your account. The call you sell pays for part of the one you buy, never all of it. The higher strike is always the cheaper call, so a bull call spread always costs money to open. We'd skip the leg you sell. We keep options simple, a plain buy once in a while.
questions.lesson_line: Net the legs first. Pay more than you collect and it's a debit.

wrong.$370 credit: Wrong direction. You paid more than you collected, so cash went out.
wrong.$870 debit: That adds the two premiums. The calls you sold pay you, so they cut the cost.

questions.simple: A $370 debit. You pay more for the calls you buy than you collect for the ones you sell.

questions.q: A friend sells 1 put at 2.80 and buys 1 lower-strike put at 1.05, same expiry. What credit lands in his account, before commissions?
questions.why: $175. He takes in 2.80 on the put he sells and pays 1.05 for the one he buys. 2.80 minus 1.05 is 1.75 a share. Times 100 shares, that's $175 in. The put he sells has the higher strike, so it's worth more, and a bull put spread always opens as a credit. That credit is his best case. The risk sits in the gap between the strikes. We don't put on credit spreads, but you should be able to read one.
questions.lesson_line: More in than out and it opens as a credit. That credit is the ceiling.
questions.simple: $175. He takes in 2.80, pays 1.05, and one contract covers 100 shares.

wrong.$385: That adds the premiums. He paid 1.05 for the lower put, so it comes off.
wrong.$280: That's only the put he sold. The one he bought costs 1.05.
wrong.$1.75: That's per share. One contract is 100 shares.

questions.story: In June you buy a call for $500 in total. By September it's worth $300, and you've lost faith in the trade.
questions.q: If you sell to close today, what's your loss, before commissions?
questions.why: $200. You paid $500 and selling gets you $300 back, and 500 minus 300 is 200. Selling is a choice you always have. The premium being your max loss doesn't mean you ride it to zero. If the idea's broken, sell what's left. Waiting costs you too, because time value wears away into expiry. Take the $200 hit and keep the $300.
questions.lesson_line: The premium is your worst case, not your only exit. Sell what's left when the idea's broken.

wrong.$500: That's the loss if you hold it to a worthless expiry. Selling now saves the $300.
wrong.$300: That's what you get back, not what you lose.
wrong.Nothing until it expires: Selling to close makes it real today. Paid $500, got $300 back, so you're down $200.

questions.simple: $200. You paid $500 and the call still sells for $300.

deeper.trap: Trap: forgetting the closing trade's cost. Commissions are charged when you close, not only when you open. The $200 loss is before those, so the real loss is larger.

questions.q: Next to the money you put in, commissions often take a bigger bite out of an options trade than a stock trade.
questions.why: True. Option premiums are small next to the price of the shares. And you pay commissions to open, to close, and on exercise or assignment. So the same fee is a much bigger slice of the trade. How big depends on your commission and the size of the premium. That's why it's often and not always. On cheap options, count the costs before you count the profit.
questions.lesson_line: On cheap options, count the costs before you count the profit.
questions.simple: True. Commissions are often big next to an option's price, so they eat more of the trade.

questions.q: You have a regular margin account. You can buy a call that expires in three months partly with borrowed money.
questions.why: False. You pay for it in full. Under FINRA's margin rule, an option you buy that expires in nine months or less needs 100 percent of its price. Spreads work the same way for the options you buy. The premium from the ones you sell can go toward the cost. Honestly that's a good thing. The cash you put up is the cash at risk, and you know it on day one.
questions.lesson_line: Short-dated options you buy are paid in full. The cash you put up is the cash at risk.
questions.simple: False. An option you buy that expires in nine months or less must be paid for in full.

questions.q: You bought 4 calls at 1.20 and sold them a week later at 2.05. What did you make, before commissions?
questions.why: $340. Exit minus entry first. 2.05 minus 1.20 is 0.85 a share. Times 100 shares, that's $85 a contract. Times 4 contracts, $340. Subtracting the 1.20 already takes out the premium you paid, so $340 is the real gain before commissions. Good trade.
questions.lesson_line: Exit minus entry, times 100, times contracts. That's your number.
questions.simple: $340. Sale price minus buy price, times 100 shares, times 4 contracts.

wrong.$820: That's what the sale brought in. Take off the 1.20 you paid.
wrong.$480: That's what you paid for the 4 calls, not what you made.

questions.story: A call shows bid 7.90, ask 8.00. You buy one contract at the ask. Nothing moves.
questions.q: You change your mind and sell it right back at the bid. What did that cost you, before commissions?
questions.why: $10. You paid the 8.00 ask, which is $800 for the contract. Selling right back gets the 7.90 bid, which is $790. 8.00 minus 7.90 is 0.10 a share, times 100 is $10. That gap is the spread, and you pay it the second you get in. Nothing has to move. On a wide spread it adds up fast. Check the bid and ask before you buy, and use a limit order.
questions.lesson_line: The spread is a cost you pay up front. Check it before you click buy.

wrong.$0.10: That's the gap per share. A contract is 100 shares.
wrong.Nothing, the price didn't move: You bought at the ask and sold at the bid. That gap costs you even when nothing moves.
wrong.$790: That's what you'd get back, not what you'd lose.

questions.simple: $10. You paid $800 at the ask and get only $790 back at the bid.

visual.title: Buy at ask, sell at bid

questions.story: Your plan risks at most $500 on this idea. The call you want is offered at 2.50. You may hold it to expiry.
questions.q: How many contracts keep your worst case at $500, before commissions?
questions.why: 2 contracts. Each costs 2.50 times 100, and held to expiry the whole premium can go.
questions.lesson_line: If you might hold to expiry, size so losing the whole premium is a loss you planned for.

wrong.4 contracts: That plans on losing only half the premium. Held to expiry, all of it can go.
wrong.200 contracts: That forgets the multiplier. Each contract costs 2.50 times 100, not 2.50.

questions.q: Your account is $50,000. You buy 4 calls at 1.50 and they expire worthless. How much of the account is gone, before commissions?
questions.why: 1.2%. Dollars first. 4 contracts, times 1.50, times 100 shares, is $600. They expired worthless, so all $600 is gone. Then the percent. 600 divided by 50,000, times 100, is 1.2%. Commissions come on top. Do this for every option you buy. Work out the premium as a share of the account before the order, because that's your real risk.
questions.lesson_line: Know the premium as a percent of your account before you buy. That's your real risk.
questions.simple: 1.2% is gone, because the calls expired worthless and you lose the whole premium you paid.

deeper.trap: Trap: thinking a cheap quote means small risk. A 1.50 quote looks small, but the 100-share contract and the number of contracts set the real dollars. Held to expiry, all of the premium can go, so size it as a loss you can take.

wrong.12%: A decimal slipped. $600 out of $50,000 is 1.2%.
wrong.6%: That's 4 times 1.50 read as a percent. You skipped the 100 shares and the account.
wrong.120%: That multiplies by 100 one time too many.

questions.story: You sell to open a 50 call for 4.00 without owning the stock. A takeover bid sends the stock to 69. The call now costs 19.00 to buy back.
questions.q: You buy it back here. What's the damage, before commissions?
questions.why: $1,500. You collected 4.00 a share, $400, when you sold it. Buying it back at 19.00 costs $1,900. 1,900 minus 400 is $1,500. Look at the shape of it. Your best case was $400. One headline turned it into a $1,500 loss, and it could have been worse. A stock has no ceiling, so a naked call has no cap on the loss. That's why we don't sell options. On the rare option we use, we're the buyer, and the premium is the most we can lose.
questions.lesson_line: On a naked call the credit caps your gain. Nothing caps the loss.

wrong.$1,900: That's the buyback. The $400 you collected comes off it.
wrong.$2,300: That adds the $400. The credit offsets the loss, it doesn't add to it.
wrong.$6,900: That's the 69 stock price times 100. You're buying back the call, not the stock.

questions.simple: $1,500. Buying back costs $1,900, and the $400 you collected covers only part of it.

deeper.trap: Trap: treating the credit as a cushion that limits the loss. The $400 offsets only part of the buyback. A stock has no price ceiling, so an uncovered call's loss is theoretically unlimited. Here a jump to 69 turned a $400 credit into a $1,500 loss.

questions.story: You bought one 100-strike call for 2.50. At expiry it's in the money, and your broker exercises it.
questions.q: Counting the call, how much cash have you put into those 100 shares, before commissions?
questions.why: $10,250. Your real price per share is the strike plus the premium. 100 plus 2.50 is 102.50, times 100 shares is $10,250. That went out in two pieces. The $250 for the call when you bought it. Then $10,000 for the shares at exercise, new cash due now. The premium isn't a down payment, so none of it comes off the $10,000. If that cash isn't ready, you have to find it fast. Plan for it before expiry, or sell the call instead.
questions.lesson_line: Exercise never refunds the premium. Your real price is strike plus premium.

wrong.$10,000: That's the exercise alone. The 2.50 you paid for the call is part of what the shares cost you.
wrong.$9,750: That treats the premium as a down payment. It isn't. The full strike is due on top.
wrong.$250: That's only the call. Exercise costs the strike times 100 on top.

questions.simple: $10,250. The shares cost the 100 strike plus the 2.50 premium, times 100 shares.

deeper.trap: Trap: forgetting the cash. Exercise needs the strike times 100, here $10,000, on top of the premium already spent. If you haven't set the cash aside, an exercise can force urgent measures to find it. Plan for it before expiry.

questions.q: A stock trades at 50. You sell the 50 put for 3.00. The company blows up and the stock goes to zero. What do you lose, before commissions?
questions.why: $4,700. You get assigned, so you buy 100 shares at the 50 strike. That's $5,000 for stock that's now worth nothing. The 3.00 you collected, $300, takes a little off. 50 minus 3, times 100, is $4,700. That's the floor, because a stock can't go below zero. But look at the trade. You risked $4,700 to make $300. Selling puts looks like easy income until the one that doesn't come back. You won't catch us on that side of it.
questions.lesson_line: A put seller's risk runs to zero. The premium only trims it.

wrong.$300: That's the premium, the buyer's worst case. The seller's risk runs all the way to zero.
wrong.$5,000: That forgets the $300 you collected. It trims the loss.
wrong.Unlimited: A stock can't fall below zero, so a put seller's loss has a floor. Here it's $4,700.

questions.simple: $4,700. Assigned, you pay 50 a share for worthless stock, and the 3.00 premium trims only a little.

deeper.counter: A put seller's worst case is the stock going to zero. Unlike an uncovered call, that loss has a floor. It is still far bigger than the premium: here $4,700 lost against $300 collected.

questions.q: A friend sold a put spread for a credit. The credit he collected is the most he can lose on it.
questions.why: False. The credit is the most he can make. His worst case is the gap between the two strikes, minus that credit. It's flipped from buying. Cash comes in now, and a bill can come later. He knows both numbers the moment he opens it. He should size off the worst case, never the credit. We stay out of these. Still, know the math, so a credit never looks like safe money to you.
questions.lesson_line: On a credit spread, the cash in is the best case. Size off the worst.
questions.simple: False. The credit is his best case, and the worst is the gap between the strikes less the credit.

deeper.trap: Trap: reading a credit as safe money. A credit spread takes cash in now in exchange for a possible outlay later. At worst the seller loses the strike gap less the credit, so that number comes first.

questions.q: You pull up a call on the chain and see its last trade price. If you buy it right now, that's the price you'll pay.
questions.why: False. You'll pay the ask. The last trade is history. It might be from this morning, or from days ago on a thin option. Premiums move all day, so the last sale can sit far from where it trades now. Look at the live bid and ask. Buying, you pay the ask. Selling, you get the bid. Set your limit off those, never off the last trade.
questions.lesson_line: Don't price an option off its last trade. Price it off the bid and ask.
questions.simple: False. Buying right now costs the ask, and the last trade may be nowhere near it.

deeper.trap: Trap: an option that last traded long ago. Its last price can sit far from today's bid and ask, because premiums change constantly. Check the live quote, and price your order off the bid and the ask, not the last trade.

questions.story: You have $5,000 and like a stock at 50. Plan one, buy 100 shares. Plan two, buy one 50 call at 5.00 and park the rest in T-bills. Plan three, buy ten 50 calls at 5.00.
questions.q: The stock is at 46 when the calls expire. Which plan lost the most?
questions.why: Ten calls, and it isn't close. At 46 a 50 call expires worthless, so all $5,000 is gone. The shares lost only the drop from 50 to 46, and you still own them. The one call lost its $500 premium, and the rest sat safe in T-bills. Same stock, same idea, three very different outcomes. What decided it was how much premium you put at risk.
questions.lesson_line: Same idea, three outcomes. How much premium you spend decides the damage.

wrong.All about the same: Same stock, same view, but very different amounts of premium at risk.
wrong.100 shares: The shares lost only the drop from 50 to 46, and you still own them.
wrong.One call, rest in T-bills: That plan risked one call's premium. The rest sat in T-bills.

questions.simple: Ten calls lost the most. All $5,000 went into calls that are worthless with the stock under 50.

deeper.example: Same view, three sizes of bet. The shares are down only the drop from 50 to 46. The one call risked its premium and kept the rest in T-bills. Ten calls put the whole $5,000 in and lose all of it at or below 50.

questions.q: You like a setup but buy a call instead of the shares. Where's your stop on the call?
questions.why: All of it. When we use an option, the premium we paid is the stop. So plan the trade as if the whole premium goes, and size it so that's a loss you can take. That's the appeal of it. Your risk is fixed the second you buy. The share-trade stop under the low of the day doesn't carry over to the call. And we only do this now and then. Most of the time we just trade the shares.
questions.simple: All of it. On an option we buy, the premium paid is the stop, so plan to lose all of it.
questions.lesson_line: On an option we buy, the premium paid is the stop. Size for losing all of it.

wrong.Half the premium paid: Don't plan on losing half. The whole premium is the stop, so size for losing all of it.
wrong.Under the stock's low: That's where a share trade's stop goes. On a call, the premium you paid is the stop.
wrong.A 3% drop in the stock: That's share-trade thinking. On the call, the stop is the premium you paid.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B25, A3, A13)

questions.q: A stock looks tired, and you think about selling calls on it without owning the shares. That's a trade we don't take.
questions.why: True. We trade shares. When we do use an option, it's only where the risk is defined. Buy a call and the premium is the most you can lose. A naked call is the opposite. A stock has no ceiling, so the loss on that call has no cap. One takeover headline and a small credit turns into a big loss. If it looks tired, just don't own it.
questions.simple: True. A naked call's loss has no ceiling, and we only use options where the risk is defined.
questions.lesson_line: We trade shares. An option stands in only when its risk is defined.

conflicts: Max loss for a call seller: FINRA says 'theoretically unlimited' (f49); OIC says 'unlimited' (f20, f17). The unit never keys a number for it: w3 says a naked call has 'no ceiling' and q21's lesson line says its loss isn't capped, which fits both wordings.

Buyer's max loss: FINRA (f48) and OIC (f21) give the premium paid; the disclosure document lists commissions as a separate cost of opening and closing (f46). q06 keys 'the premium you paid, plus commissions', and every dollar question says 'before commissions'.

Contract size after corporate actions: the disclosure document's 3-for-2 example adjusts a contract to 150 shares at a new strike, while its 1-for-10 reverse split example keeps the 100 multiplier for the price and changes only the shares delivered. The dollar math on adjusted contracts differs case by case, so this unit computes every premium on a standard 100-share contract and never on an adjusted one. That the 100-share rule has exceptions belongs to F6.01.

q06 keys the official buyer rule (FINRA f48, OIC f21): the premium is the most the option itself can lose. If an in-the-money call is exercised into shares, those shares are a new position with their own risk (FINRA's options page also warns about pin risk at expiry). q22 teaches that exercised shares cost the strike plus the premium; exercise risk belongs to F6.16.
OIC's Long Call page shows a stray header line copied from its butterfly page; the cited lines (f21, f22, f23) are in the Long Call page's own body text.

q16 is asked for a regular (strategy-based) margin account. FINRA 4210(g) portfolio margin is 'an alternative to the "strategy-based" margin requirements' for approved accounts: the requirement is the portfolio's greatest theoretical loss, with a per-contract minimum 'not to exceed the market value in the case of long contracts', so a long option there can need less than 100 percent. The unit does not teach portfolio margin; a cash account pays in full anyway.
